correctness.rationale: All \(2\times2\) and \(3\times3\) strict preference profiles are exhausted. Every perfect matching is checked by two independent blocking-pair tests, objective values are exact integer rank sums, and the complete argmin sets are compared without tie-breaking. The published stable-count marginal is reproduced, and the explicit witness has exactly the two stated stable matchings.

evidence: Iwama, Miyazaki, and Yanagisawa define egalitarian and sex-equalness costs and study sex-equal approximation, including an egalitarian secondary objective.
De Clercq et al. provide an exact framework able to optimize sex-equal and egalitarian stable matchings.
Bistarelli and Santini explicitly display the standard formulas for egalitarian and sex-equal costs.
Borodin et al. enumerate three-pair stable-matching counts and egalitarian-cost statistics but do not tabulate sex-equal optima.
broader_coverage.reasoning: These broader works establish the objectives and surrounding algorithms but do not imply the exact relationship of their complete argmin sets on every \(3\times3\) profile. In particular, NP-hardness of sex-equal optimization and polynomial solvability of egalitarian optimization do not determine their first finite conflict.

originality.rationale: Prior work defines and algorithmically studies egalitarian and sex-equal stable marriage, while later small-instance work enumerates stable counts and egalitarian-cost statistics. No inspected source states the four-way exact \(3\times3\) argmin-set relation census or the sharp first disjointness boundary at three pairs.
residual_risks: An unindexed thesis, exercise, note, or software enumeration may contain the same three-pair relation table.
The originality conclusion is based on targeted semantic and exact-count searches plus inspection of the closest primary sources, not a proof of bibliographic uniqueness.
The result makes no structural or asymptotic claim for markets larger than three pairs.

value.rationale: Egalitarian and sex-equal stable marriage are standard fairness criteria representing total welfare burden and inter-side balance. Their first possible incompatibility is a natural boundary question. The exact three-pair census distinguishes equality, both strict-inclusion directions, and disjointness, giving substantially more structure than a lone counterexample.
